title: Lester Young as the most influential tenor player
summary: Edison says Lester treated the bandstand as a proving ground, and describes 300 one-nighters a year.

story.theme_name: Lester Young: the man, the sound, the Basie years
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: Let's go back to Basie now, where we left off with Lester and company. Because we want -- what I was

Well, getting back to him, I don't think there's nobody in the world that was more influential to the tenor players nowadays than Lester Young. I think he was the most influential, more than Coleman Hawkins, more than anybody that I know of right now.

Today. He's the most influential. And he will try anything on the bandstand. He liked to -- he would -- anything that he thought he wanted to try, he would try. Because he maintained that if you didn't try it on the bandstand, where you going to try it? You know, if it doesn't work in that instance, you know it's not going to work there, but you keep playing it until it does work. It's like an experiment, you know. And the bandstand was a proving ground to him. Like it was to most of us, you know. Because we worked so much until -- we used to do like 300 one-nighters a year, you know, because we had no place to play. Jimmy Lunceford at the Cotton Club and after they come out of the Cotton Club, he would go on like 40 weeks of a circuit, theaters, you know. And Basie, 40 weeks of one-nighters.
